messages.text:
Yes. I think the architecture should **deliberately prevent continuous integration**.

If every agent continuously shares everything into one context, you get a cognitive version of strong mode coupling: synchronization, correlated errors, and eventually one beige consensus representation. What you want instead is closer to condensed matter:

\[
\boxed{
\text{long-lived independent modes}
+
\text{sparse, event-triggered coupling}
+
\text{occasional collective transitions}
}
\]

The swarm's **communication topology itself should be part of the experiment**.

## 1. Give each agent a different representational basis

Don't merely give them different job titles. Give them different *state spaces*.

For the same candidate lattice \(x\):

\[
x\rightarrow
\begin{cases}
z_{\rm spectral} & \{\omega_i,\phi_i,\rho(\omega)\}\\
z_{\rm transport} & \{G^R,S,T_{ij}\}\\
z_{\rm topology} & \{\nu,W_\gamma,\text{edge states}\}\\
z_{\rm geometry} & \{\text{motifs,symmetries,defects}\}\\
z_{\rm localization} & \{\mathrm{IPR},\xi\}\\
z_{\rm dynamics} & \{\tau,Q,\text{transients}\}\\
z_{\rm human} & \text{human-interpretable mechanism}
\end{cases}
\]

Crucially, **the spectral agent shouldn't automatically see the topology agent's interpretation**.

Otherwise you've contaminated the supposedly independent representation.

Each agent should maintain its own:

\[
\boxed{\text{local world model + local QD archive + local anomaly list}.}
\]

That's genuine representational diversity.

---

# 2. Communication should mostly consist of **queries and counterexamples**

Not transcripts.

Agent A shouldn't send:

> “Here's everything I've been thinking for 12,000 tokens.”

Instead it publishes something like:

> **Artifact #817**
>
> Candidates \(x_{391}\) and \(x_{827}\) are almost indistinguishable under my spectral representation:
>
> \[
> d_{\rm spectrum}(391,827)<0.002
> \]
>
> but Transport Agent reports
>
> \[
> d_{\rm transport}(391,827)=0.81.
> \]
>
> **Unresolved question:** What invariant distinguishes them?

Now topology, gauge, geometry, and nonlinear agents can independently attack that **specific discrepancy**.

Communication becomes scientific.

---

# 3. The most important communication trigger should be **representational disagreement**

This gives you a beautiful mathematical trigger.

Each representation \(r\) defines a distance:

\[
d_r(x_i,x_j).
\]

Now look for pairs where representations disagree:

\[
\Delta_{rs}(i,j)
=
\left|
\tilde d_r(i,j)-\tilde d_s(i,j)
\right|.
\]

Large

\[
\Delta_{rs}
\]

means:

> **These two scientific languages disagree about whether these materials are different.**

That's precisely where agents should communicate.

For example:

\[
d_{\rm spectrum}(A,B)\approx0
\]

but

\[
d_{\rm routing}(A,B)\gg0.
\]

Don't merge the agents.

Trigger a **temporary interdisciplinary coalition**:

\[
\{\text{spectral},\text{gauge},\text{transport}\}.
\]

Their task:

> Find the minimal additional descriptor explaining the discrepancy.

Maybe they discover signed loop flux.

Then the coalition dissolves.

That is much better than a permanent committee.

---

# 4. Spectral diversity can determine **who talks to whom**

Here's the especially fun part.

Represent each agent's recent scientific behavior by a feature vector:

\[
h_a.
\]

Construct an agent similarity graph

\[
W_{ab}
=
\operatorname{sim}(h_a,h_b).
\]

Compute its graph Laplacian:

\[
L=D-W.
\]

Then examine its eigenvectors.

If all agents' activity collapses into a few dominant eigendirections, your swarm is becoming representationally homogeneous.

You could measure an effective spectral diversity:

\[
D_{\rm agent}
=
\exp\left(
-\sum_k p_k\log p_k
\right),
\qquad
p_k=\frac{\lambda_k}{\sum_j\lambda_j}.
\]

Or use singular values of the matrix of agent embeddings/descriptors/hypotheses.

Now the coordinator has an explicit objective:

\[
\boxed{
\text{maintain enough spectral diversity among agents}
}
\]

without simply maximizing disagreement.

---

# 5. But don't maximize agent diversity blindly

This is exactly analogous to our material problem.

Twenty completely orthogonal agents that never exchange useful information are useless.

Twenty identical agents are also useless.

So the target is something like:

\[
\mathcal J=
D_{\rm representation}
+
\alpha D_{\rm mechanism}
+
\beta I_{\rm useful\ cross-talk}
-
\gamma R_{\rm redundancy}.
\]

The sweet spot is:

\[
\boxed{
\text{independent enough to discover different things}
\atop
\text{coupled enough to exploit complementarities}.
}
\]

That is literally the same optimization we're applying to the materials.

---

# 6. I would create **resonance conditions** for communication

Agents communicate when one of several events occurs:

**Contradiction resonance.** Two representations strongly disagree.

\[
d_A(x,y)\ll1,\qquad d_B(x,y)\gg1.
\]

**Anomaly resonance.** A candidate lies far outside an agent's learned manifold.

\[
\operatorname{OOD}_A(x)>\tau.
\]

**Boundary resonance.** A candidate sits near a phase / behavioral transition.

**Uncertainty resonance.** An agent predicts large epistemic uncertainty.

**Complementarity resonance.** Another agent possesses information predicted to reduce that uncertainty.

**Stagnation resonance.** One archive hasn't acquired a genuinely new niche for \(N\) generations.

**Tradeoff-breaking resonance.** Something appears to violate the existing Pareto frontier.

Those are the moments where interdisciplinary communication has high expected value.

---

# 7. And then use an **information-gain router**

Before agent \(A\) asks agent \(B\), estimate:

\[
\mathrm{VOI}(A\leftarrow B)
=
\frac{
\mathbb E[\Delta\text{scientific information}]
}{
\text{communication cost}
}.
\]

Only open the channel if

\[
\mathrm{VOI}>\tau.
\]

That means your communication graph is dynamic:

\[
G_{\rm swarm}(t).
\]

Most edges are absent most of the time.

That's exactly analogous to the rare-coupling material architecture:

\[
g_{ij}(t)\approx0
\]

until a resonance criterion occurs.

Then:

\[
g_{ij}(t^\star)\gg0.
\]

---

# 8. I'd introduce **scientific synapses**

Every pair of agents gets a slowly evolving coupling weight:

\[
J_{ab}.
\]

Initially, perhaps:

\[
J_{ab}\sim\text{sparse random}.
\]

After communication event \(e\), measure its scientific yield:

\[
Y_e=
\Delta\text{coverage}
+
\Delta\text{prediction}
+
\Delta\text{novel mechanism}
-
\text{cost}.
\]

Then:

\[
J_{ab}(t+1)
=
J_{ab}(t)+\eta Y_e.
\]

If Gauge Agent repeatedly helps Transport Agent explain anomalies, that channel strengthens.

If Geometry Agent and Spectrum Agent mostly tell each other things they already know, their channel weakens.

So the **social topology of the scientists self-organizes around productive interdisciplinarity**.

---

# 9. But add an anti-echo-chamber term

Otherwise the same successful little clique eventually dominates.

So penalize excessive communication concentration:

\[
\mathcal L_{\rm social}
=
-\text{scientific yield}
+
\lambda\,\text{communication concentration}.
\]

You could enforce something akin to exploration:

occasionally connect agents with

\[
J_{ab}\approx0
\]

precisely because they almost never interact.

Call these **cross-modal probes**.

Most will produce nothing.

Occasionally:

\[
\text{tensegrity agent}
+
\text{gauge agent}
\]

notices something neither community would have considered.

That's the agent equivalent of a rare nonlinear mode coupling.

---

# 10. Even better: have **different timescales of integration**

This is probably important.

### Fast scale: isolation

Agents run many local experiments independently.

\[
\tau_{\rm local}\sim1
\]

### Medium scale: pairwise resonance

Two or three agents communicate around a specific anomaly.

\[
\tau_{\rm coalition}\sim10
\]

### Slow scale: global synthesis

The entire swarm periodically updates the shared ontology.

\[
\tau_{\rm global}\sim100
\]

So you deliberately impose:

\[
\tau_{\rm local}
\ll
\tau_{\rm coalition}
\ll
\tau_{\rm global}.
\]

That prevents global consensus from continuously erasing local novelty.

It's essentially **multiscale cognition**.

---

# 11. The shared memory should also be stratified

Don't have one giant blackboard.

Have three layers.

### Private memory

Each agent keeps:

- hypotheses
- failed ideas
- representations
- local archive
- uncertainties

Nobody else automatically sees it.

### Published evidence

Agents publish only:

\[
\{\text{claim, artifact, simulation, uncertainty, counterexample}\}.
\]

This is the scientific literature layer.

### Shared ontology

Very slowly changing:

\[
\mathcal S_t.
\]

Contains accepted types like:

- Mode
- LoopFlux
- Localization
- ResolventChannel
- GaugeEquivalence
- TransportPhenotype

Changing this layer requires stronger evidence.

This fits the Wang-Buehler/copresheaf idea beautifully.

---

# 12. Then you get **local schema forks**

This may be even more important than local memories.

Suppose Gauge Agent thinks:

\[
\texttt{LoopFlux}
\]

is fundamental.

Spectral Agent thinks:

\[
\texttt{ModeHybridization}
\]

is the correct representation.

Don't immediately decide.

Allow:

\[
\mathcal S^{(A)}
\]

and

\[
\mathcal S^{(B)}
\]

to coexist.

Let both generate predictions.

Later, maybe:

\[
\mathcal S^{(A)}
\]

explains routing,

while

\[
\mathcal S^{(B)}
\]

explains localization.

Then the synthesis isn't necessarily

\[
A\text{ wins}.
\]

It may be:

\[
\mathcal S^{(C)}
=
\text{some composition of A and B}.
\]

This is **representational speciation**.

That's much closer to biological/ecological diversity than ordinary multi-agent debate.

---

# 13. QD should apply to the agents' *representations*, too

We previously had a QD archive of materials.

Add another archive:

\[
\boxed{\text{QD archive of scientific representations}.}
\]

A representation gets descriptors such as:

\[
(
\text{predictive accuracy},
\text{compression},
\text{invariance},
\text{interpretability},
\text{robustness},
\text{novel distinctions}
).
\]

Now you preserve:

- a very compressed representation,
- a highly predictive representation,
- an interpretable representation,
- a topology-sensitive representation,
- a transport-sensitive representation.

Instead of demanding one universal latent space.

That's huge.

---

# 14. And then there are actually **three coupled QD archives**

This is the architecture I'd propose now:

\[
\boxed{
\mathcal A_{\rm matter}
\leftrightarrow
\mathcal A_{\rm representation}
\leftrightarrow
\mathcal A_{\rm swarm}
}
\]

### Matter archive

What physically different behaviors exist?

### Representation archive

What scientific languages best distinguish/explain them?

### Swarm archive

What communication structures most efficiently discover them?

Now each level evolves the others.

A weird material breaks the current representation.

A new representation reveals a previously invisible material niche.

A new communication topology makes that representation discoverable.

This becomes genuinely open-ended.

---

# 15. Spectral methods can decide **when integration is necessary**

Suppose the agents produce different representations:

\[
Z_1,Z_2,\ldots,Z_N.
\]

Calculate something like canonical correlations, mutual information, kernel alignment, or principal angles between their subspaces.

If:

\[
Z_A\approx Z_B,
\]

don't make them talk.

They're redundant.

If:

\[
Z_A\perp Z_B
\]

but both predict different aspects of behavior well, preserve them separately.

If:

\[
Z_A\perp Z_B
\]

and a particular anomaly requires both,

**that's exactly when you integrate them.**

So:

\[
\boxed{
\text{integration should be anomaly-conditioned, not continuous}.
}
\]

That's probably the sentence I would put in the hackathon proposal.

---

# 16. The hackathon implementation can actually be quite small

You don't need 50 agents.

Start with **six**:

1. Geometry
2. Spectrum
3. Gauge/topology
4. Transport/resolvent
5. QD/archive
6. Skeptic/schema-breaker

Each gets:

\[
\text{private context}
+
\text{private descriptor}
+
\text{private candidate ranking}.
\]

They are prohibited from continuously sharing internal states.

Every candidate goes through the simulator.

Then calculate pairwise **representation disagreement**.

Only the largest disagreement triggers a temporary 2–3 agent coalition.

That coalition receives:

\[
\text{candidate}
+
\text{published evidence}
+
\text{specific discrepancy}
\]

and must return:

\[
\boxed{
\text{new descriptor}
\quad\text{OR}\quad
\text{new experiment}
\quad\text{OR}\quad
\text{proof of equivalence}.
}
\]

That is beautifully concrete.

---

## And it gives you a killer ablation

Compare:

\[
\textbf{A:}
\quad
\text{one giant agent}
\]

versus

\[
\textbf{B:}
\quad
\text{six agents continuously sharing everything}
\]

versus

\[
\textbf{C:}
\quad
\text{six isolated agents with no communication}
\]

versus

\[
\boxed{
\textbf{D:}
\quad
\text{six representationally diverse agents with event-triggered communication}.
}
\]

Hold total inference tokens and solver calls constant.

Measure:

\[
\text{validated behavioral niches discovered}
\]

\[
\text{representation diversity}
\]

\[
\text{false novelty}
\]

\[
\text{false merging}
\]

\[
\text{new useful descriptors}
\]

\[
\text{solver calls / discovery}.
\]

Your hypothesis is **not**:

> multi-agent > single-agent.

It's much sharper:

\[
\boxed{
\textbf{strategically coupled representational diversity}
>
\textbf{permanent consensus OR permanent isolation}.
}
\]

And wonderfully, that is **the exact same hypothesis you're testing about the material itself**:

\[
\boxed{
\text{diverse modes}
+
\text{selective coupling}
>
\text{everything coupled}
\quad\text{or}\quad
\text{nothing coupled}.
}
\]

So the swarm becomes a computational analogue of the material it is searching.

That recursion could be the conceptual centerpiece of the Buehler hackathon submission.
